newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean workers bust barricades, strikers warned.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean workers bust barricades, strikers warned.

text.p: Hyundai shipyard workers broke through picket lines on Wednesday, dodging fists and buckets of paint hurled by unionists to keep open South Korea's biggest dockyard and defy a call for nationwide strikes.

Prosecutors told striking workers to stop industrial action immediately or face arrest and warned that North Korea might try to exploit the crisis over a controverisal new labour law rammed through parliament on December 26.
Cabinet ministers said the strikes were damaging the economy and added that the government was ready for any repercussions from the arrest of union leaders sheltering in a Seoul cathedral.

"North Korea is agitating workers to topple the government," prosecutor Choi Byung-kook told a news conference. "If the unrest drags on it will give North Korea an opportunity for revolutionary struggle.
"If labour unrest continues, it will deal a serious blow to the nation's economy and the people's daily lives," he said.

In the southeast city of Ulsan, a hotbed of union militancy, several hundred strikers blocking the iron gates of the giant Hyundai facility tossed yellow paint as non-union workers in blue overalls surged through.
Later, strike-breakers used bulldozers to smash down barricades at the shipyard entrance.

Cabinet ministers said seizing leaders of the outlawed Korean Confederation of Trade Unions "cannot be delayed", a statement from the Prime Minister's Office said. The prosecution has arrest warrants on seven unionists.

Seoul was largely unaffected by the nationwide strike call by the confederation and the officially-sanctioned Federation of Korean Trade Unions. Buses and subways ran normally, although some taxi drivers stayed at home.

The unions had called for the biggest strike ever in South Korea on Tuesday and Wednesday, intending to cap three weeks of sporadic stoppages over the law, which breaks a tradition of jobs-for-life by permitting layoffs.
But the confederation, citing public concern, backed away from an all-out public sector strike call, instead urging partial strikes in key services as well as industrial walkouts.
President Kim Young-sam argues that flexible labour practices will cut corporate costs and improve South Korea's international competitiveness.

The South Korean currency, the won, took a battering over fears that prolonged strikes could threaten already slowing export growth. The government sounded an alarm over the outlook for the trade deficit.
Trade Minister Ahn Kwang-koo warned that the stoppages, which have hurt firms crucial to the export-led economy, could make it harder to control a snowballing trade deficit.
Last year's deficit stood at $20 billion. Worries that the deficit could spin further out of control sent the won plunging to a new six-year low on Wednesday.
The government forecast on Wednesdsay gross domestic product growth of about six percent for 1997, compared with an estimated 6.9 percent for last year.
Stock investors, however, were relieved that the latest round of strikes was fizzling and sent share prices up for the second day.
"Korea Telecom, the postal service and the nation's railroad services have not been influenced by the strike," a labour ministry official said.
Television showed commuters boarding buses, and subway trains pulling into stations even though 2,000 underground rail workers were on strike.
Operators of the Seoul subway have said non-union drivers can keep the system operating for two weeks.
The Labour Ministry said only three of Seoul's 88 bus companies had observed the strike call and bus services elsewhere were normal.
The decision to go ahead with arrests of the seven unionists camped in a tent at Myongdong Cathedral was taken at a meeting of ministers presided over by Prime Minister Lee Soo-sung.
"The meeting confirmed the government's position that the arrest of the leaders of illegal strikes cannot be delayed even with some negative effects and repercussions," a ministry statement said.
